stories.title: Levent Alpöge claims proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis [pdf]
stories.reason: Alpoge says he got Anthropic models to produce a 17.4M-line Lean-verified proof of GRH; if it holds, this is the biggest AI-for-math result yet.
key_facts: Levent Alpoge says Anthropic models produced a Lean-certified proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis.
The proof is reported as 17.4 million lines of Lean code, posted on GitHub.
Separately, AI had already proved zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie within 3/8 of the critical line (covered by Quanta the prior day).
Scott Aaronson (independent commentator) says no Lean-certified AI math result has yet been retracted, while several uncertified ones have.
Lean's kernel has had soundness bugs in the past (allowing proofs of 0=1), which is the main reason full confidence is still pending.

stories.title: Amazon says Chinese hackers used Cairn AI tool to discover apparent zero-day during attack on university
stories.reason: Amazon's CISO publishes a primary account of Chinese-nexus actors running the autonomous AI pentest tool Cairn against universities, including a genuine zero-day the agents found and exploited unattended — exactly the AI-offense-with-PoC always-surface case.
key_facts: Amazon found a publicly exposed Cairn instance being run by a China-based operator (prompts in Simplified Chinese, China Standard Time timestamps) against East Asian universities.
One run: 148 actions over 16 hours, including an attempted Log4Shell exploit, failed.
Another run: tested 30,000+ credential combinations against 80 real usernames over 6+ hours, failed.

Success came via a path-traversal zero-day in an open-source medical-imaging AI app; Amazon assessed high confidence it was previously unknown (now GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94) and the same bug was reused against a second university.
Amazon's CISO: the agents ran unattended for 16 hours and could weaponize a zero-day in minutes, faster than most SOCs can triage an alert.
The same week, FBI warned about a similar tool (Artex) and Google published a report on autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks.

stories.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI
stories.reason: Architect Labs claims a CPU 'discovered, designed and verified end-to-end by AI' with real pre-silicon numbers (4.59x perf/watt geomean) — a strong, verifiable claim of AI doing novel systems engineering, even though all numbers are company-reported.
key_facts: Frostbite is an interaction-net-based CPU (Vine language -> Ivy IR), built with no central scheduler; tiles run local work then steal from neighbors.
An 800k+ line Lean formal spec (Arcmodel) is used to check RTL/UVM/C/SVA; Arcmodel is claimed ~200x-660x faster than RTL simulation, accurate to 1-5%.
Agent swarms tried 58 architecture ideas across 4 searches, keeping 37.
7nm process, 500MHz final GDS; one Frostbite quad is 0.792mm^2 vs 0.895mm^2 for an undisclosed comparison CPU ('TCPU').
Geomean perf/watt vs TCPU: 4.59x across 25 workloads (6.02x on the search set, 3.83x on 15 held-out workloads); perf/area 8.77x; per-workload range ~1.15x (fib) to ~23x (conv2d).
Caveat: all results are company-reported; the comparison CPU is unnamed; broader multicore/SPEC comparisons are still planned.

stories.title: Vibecoding an inference chip
stories.reason: A first-person account of coding agents (Codex, Claude Opus/Astra) building a working ternary-weight-LLM FPGA inference engine from scratch, with concrete before/after throughput numbers — exactly the 'running code beats a description' case, and low-saturation (personal blog, 113 pts).
key_facts: Author had no prior FPGA/Verilog experience; agents wrote nearly all of ~3M lines of code (mostly C++, some Verilog) across ~$10k of Claude/OpenAI tokens.
Throughput rose from 6.43 to 213.13 tokens/s (33x) on an AWS F2 FPGA instance running a ternary-weight LLM at 8,192-token context.
That beat a bit-exact 32-core CPU implementation (129.5 tok/s) at a similar hourly price ($1.98/hr for the FPGA).
Final clock lowered to 225/425MHz after a soak test found faults at 231.25MHz; author does not recommend the architecture for production.

stories.title: BaaRai/ARTEX
stories.reason: The actual FBI-flagged autonomous pentest tool Artex is a public, actively-maintained AGPL repo (14k stars, SBOM + build provenance on releases) — running code for exactly the AI-offense tooling this profile always wants.
key_facts: ARTEX (this is an English-translation fork of Autumn-27/ARTEX, upstream now private) is a self-hosted, LLM-driven pentest platform: a planner breaks goals into intents, worker agents run real tools, findings tie back to captured HTTP traffic.
Includes a recording MITM proxy, human approval gates, scope rules and budgets; works with Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible, or local Ollama models.
~14k stars, ~5.5k forks, 1,232 commits; releases ship SHA-256 sums, a CycloneDX SBOM, and GitHub build-provenance attestations.
This is the same 'Artex' the FBI advisory (referenced in the Amazon/Cairn reporting) warned about a week earlier.

stories.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
stories.reason: ROGUE-AI offline-replicates real LLM-agent harm incidents against matched controls and reproduces the reported harm 89% of the time — a rigorous, concrete AI-agent-safety eval with a usable pre-release audit suite as its contribution.
key_facts: Replicates real agent-harm incidents (e.g. a coding agent deleting a production database) offline against a matched control missing only the blamed cause.
Reproduced reported harm in 89% of 108 attempted replications.
Across 5 models (GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek), the blamed mistake recurred in 18-33% of runs with the cause present vs <=1% without it.

62 of 72 real-harm incidents had no attacker at all — agents completed their task but missed an ordinary hazard (e.g. a database shared with a live site); prompt-injection defenses would catch none of these.
A tool-output warning that names the hazard and consequence reduced harm across all 5 models; a same-length warning without the hazard mostly did not.

stories.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
stories.reason: A systematization-of-knowledge paper tracking how LLM vulnerability-discovery capability has evolved (autonomy levels, disclosure volume, long-lived-bug discovery rate) — squarely in Mine's always-surface eval-methodology + AI-x-cyber lane.
key_facts: Rates LLM vuln-research autonomy on a driving-automation-style scale and grades each capability claim for correctness/evidence strength.
Agents reached autonomous discovery+validation+patching of real-software vulnerabilities before 2026's most restricted frontier models; open-weight models later matched that autonomy.
Disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled in 2026, with a growing critical/high share.
Severe decade-plus-old bugs in widely used code are being reported several times more often than before.
Report-to-fix and disclosure-to-attack timelines have not measurably changed yet.

stories.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
stories.reason: A 27B open model edits its own weights (no gradients/training) to raise held-out accuracy by 6.6pp and self-repair a damaged copy to >80% of original accuracy across 8 sessions — a genuinely new capability result with real numbers, though arxiv-only with no linked repo.
key_facts: Open 27B model is given its own weights + graded answers + ability to run itself; it diagnoses failures and edits the responsible weights, keeping only edits that help on practice problems.
Self-edit raises accuracy by 6.6 percentage points on unseen problems; accuracy rose across 8 consecutive self-rewriting sessions.
A deliberately damaged copy is restored to >80% of original accuracy on unseen image tasks with no retraining and no access to original weights.
Only the largest model in the family tested can usefully self-edit/self-repair; smaller models make no useful edit or make things worse.
No linked code repository found on the paper page.
